When Moses (peace be upon him) fell upon the ground, a light between his eyes overwhelmed her; every joint of her body trembled, and love for Moses (peace be upon him) entered her heart. Then she said to her: "O woman, I did not come to you when you called me except that my intention was to kill your newborn and inform Pharaoh. But I have found for this son of yours a love such as I have never found for anything like it. So guard [in the Isfahan manuscript: "guard for me"] your son, for I see that he is our enemy."

When the midwife left her, some of the spies saw her and came to her door to enter upon Moses' mother. Her sister said: "O mother, the guards are at the door!" So she wrapped Moses in a cloth and placed him in the oven, which was lit. Her mind was confused and she did not know what she was doing. They entered and found the oven lit, and they saw that Moses' mother's color had not changed, and no milk had appeared for her. They said: "Who was it that entered upon you, the midwife?" She said: "She is a close friend of mine; she entered upon me as a visitor." So they left her. Her reason returned to her, and she said to Moses' sister: "Where is the child?" She said: "I do not know." Then she heard the child's crying from the oven, so she went to it, and God had made the fire cool and safe for him, and she took him up.

He said: Then, when Moses' mother (peace be upon him) saw Pharaoh's insistence on seeking out the infants, she feared for her son. So God cast into her soul that she should make for him a chest, and then cast the chest into the river, which is the Nile. She went to a carpenter from Egypt, from the people of Pharaoh, and bought a small chest from him. The carpenter said to her: "What will you do with this chest?" She said: "I have a son whom I wish to hide in the chest." She disliked lying. He said: "And why?" She said: "I fear for him the plot of Pharaoh." When she had bought the chest and carried it away, the carpenter went to those slaughterers to inform them of the matter of Moses' mother. When he began to speak, God Most High held his tongue so that he could not speak, and he began to gesture with his hand. The officials did not understand what he meant. When they were unable to make out his matter, their chief said: "Strike him!" So they struck him and drove him out.

When the carpenter reached his place, God Most High returned his tongue to him, and he spoke. He set out again, intending to go to the officials to inform them, but God Most High took away his tongue and his sight, so he could not speak and could not see anything. They struck him and drove him out, and he fell into a valley in which there were wild beasts. He made a vow to God that if He returned his tongue and sight, he would not point Him out [i.e., the child], and would be with him to protect him wherever he was. God, Mighty and Majestic, knew from him his sincerity, so He returned his sight and his tongue to him. He fell down prostrate before God and said: "O Lord, guide me to this righteous servant!" God guided him to him. He came out of the valley, believed in him, affirmed him, and knew that this was from God.

Then Moses' mother set out and cast him into the sea. Pharaoh had at that time a daughter, who was his only child, and she was among the most honored of people to him. Every day she had three requests that she would raise to Pharaoh, and she had severe leprosy, a scaly leprosy. Pharaoh had gathered for her the physicians and magicians of Egypt, and they examined her case and said to him: "O King, she will not be cured except from the direction of the sea, where something resembling a human is found; some of its saliva should be taken and smeared on her leprosy, and she will be healed from it. That will be on such-and-such a day, at such-and-such an hour, when the sun rises."

When Monday came, Pharaoh went out to a council he had on the bank of the Nile, and with him was Asiya, daughter of Muzahim. The daughter of Pharaoh came with her maidens and sat on the shore of the Nile with her maidens, playing with them and sprinkling water on their faces. Suddenly the Nile brought the chest, tossed by the waves. Pharaoh said: "This thing in the sea has caught on the tree; bring it to me!" They rushed to it with boats from every side until they placed it before him. They tried to open the lid but could not; they tried to break it but could not.

He said [in the Isfahan manuscript: "She said"]: Then Asiya drew near and saw inside the chest a light that no one but her saw, because of what God Most High willed to honor her with. She worked at it and opened the lid, and behold, there was a small child in his cradle, and a light between his eyes. God Most High had placed his provision in his thumb, which he sucked for milk. God Most High cast love for Moses (peace be upon him) into Asiya's heart, and Pharaoh loved him and was tender toward him. The daughter of Pharaoh came; when they took the child out of the chest, she went to what was flowing from his saliva and smeared it on her leprosy, and she was healed. She kissed him and pressed him to her breast.

The fools among Pharaoh's people said: "O King, we think that this infant is the one of the Children of Israel whom we fear; he was cast into the sea out of fear of you. Kill him!" Pharaoh resolved to kill him [in the Isfahan manuscript: "When he resolved to kill him"]. Asiya said: ﴿A delight of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son.﴾ She was barren, so she asked Pharaoh to give Moses to her, and he gave him to her. Pharaoh said: "As for me, I have no need of him."

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) [in the Isfahan manuscript: "may God bless him and grant him peace"] said:

"If Pharaoh had said on that day, 'He is a delight of the eye for me as he is for you,' as his wife said, God would have guided him as He guided her. But God, Mighty and Majestic, willed to deprive him of it, because of what had preceded in God's knowledge." [126] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 2/34, no. 3022.]

It was said to Asiya: "Name him." She said: "I named him Musha, because we found him in water and trees. So 'Mu' is water, and 'sha' is tree."

This is His saying, Glorified be He: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾, i.e., took him. The Arabs say of something that came upon them suddenly, without seeking or intending it: "I found it by iltiqat (chance-finding)," and "I met so-and-so by iltiqat." From this comes the word luqatah (a found object), which is what is found lost and then taken. ﴿That he might be for them an enemy and a grief﴾: this lam is called lam al-'aqibah (the lam of consequence) or lam al-sayrurah (the lam of outcome), because they took him intending that he would be a delight for them, but the outcome of that was that he became for them an enemy and a grief. The poet said:

"So for death the mothers raise their young, as for the ruin of houses, dwellings are built."

[Lisan al-'Arab: 12/562.]

As for "an enemy and a grief," the people of Kufa read it with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the zay, while the others read it with a fatha on both ha' and zay. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, saying it is for emphasis. There was disagreement about it apart from 'Asim. They are two dialects, like 'adam and 'adam, and suqm and suqm.

﴿Indeed Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts were sinners﴾: sinful, guilty.

﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said: A delight of the eye.﴾ That is: he is a delight of the eye ﴿for me and for you. Do not kill him, for God has brought him to us from another land and he is not from the Children of Israel. Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son.﴾ ﴿And they did not perceive﴾ what would come to pass from their affair and his. This is from Mujahid and Qatadah. ﴿And they did not perceive﴾: their destruction would be at his hands. Muhammad ibn Zakariyya [in the Isfahan manuscript: "Muhammad ibn Ishaq"] ibn Yasar said: ﴿And they did not perceive﴾: "I do what I will, and I do not do what they want."

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Talhah and 'Ubayd Allah narrated to us, both saying: Abu Mujahid narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Harb told me, saying: Sunayd narrated to us,

saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Abu Ma'shar [in the Isfahan manuscript: "from Abu Ma'sar"], from Muhammad ibn Qays: ﴿And they did not perceive﴾ means: the Children of Israel did not know that We had picked him up [in the Isfahan manuscript: "picked them up"]. Al-Kalbi said: ﴿And they did not perceive﴾ except that he was our son.

﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void﴾, i.e., empty, careless, heedless of everything except the remembrance of Moses and concern for him. This is what most exegetes said. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ishaq, and Ibn Zayd said: it means void of the revelation that God Most High had revealed to her when He commanded her to cast him into the sea, and not to fear or grieve, and the promise We made to her that We would return him to her and make him one of the messengers. Then Satan came to her and said: "O mother of Moses, you disliked that Pharaoh should kill Moses, so that you would have his reward and recompense, and you yourself undertook to kill him, casting him into the sea and drowning him."

When news reached her that Pharaoh had found him in the Nile, she said: "He has fallen into the hands of his enemy, the very one from whom I fled with him!" The overwhelming trial made her forget what God had promised her. God Most High said: ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void﴾ of the revelation that had been revealed to her. Al-Kisa'i said: "Void" means forgetful. Abu 'Ubaydah said: ﴿void﴾ of grief, because she knew he had not drowned. It is from the Arabs' saying: "blood is fargh (void)" when it is wasted, with neither retaliation nor blood-money for it. The poet said:

"If camels were taken from you, and women, you will not leave them void, without killing your captives."

[Al-Sihah: 4/1665; Lisan al-'Arab: 11/141.]

Al-'Ala' ibn Zayd said: "farighan" means fleeing. Ibn Muhaysin and Fadalah ibn 'Ubayd read it as fazi'an (anxious), with a zay and an 'ayn, without an alif.

﴿Had she not nearly disclosed him﴾. Some said: the pronoun in "bihi" (of him) refers back to Moses, and the meaning is: she nearly disclosed that he was her son, from the intensity of her grief.

Abu Bakr 'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Warraq informed us, saying: Makki ibn 'Abdan informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Bishr narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Sa'id, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Had she not nearly disclosed him﴾, he said: she nearly said, "Woe, my son!" Muqatil said: When she saw the chest being lifted by one wave and set down by another, she feared he would drown, and she nearly cried out from her compassion [in the Isfahan manuscript: "her compassion"] for him. Al-Kalbi said: She nearly showed that he was her son, and that was when she heard the people saying to Moses after he had grown up: "Moses, son of Pharaoh!" It grieved her, and she nearly said: "No, rather he is my son."

Some said: the pronoun refers back to the revelation, meaning: had she not nearly disclosed the revelation by which We revealed to her that We would return him to her.

﴿Had We not bound fast her heart﴾: We strengthened her heart, protected her, and made her firm, ﴿so that she would be among the believers﴾, those who affirm and are certain of the promise of God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And Moses' mother said to his sister﴾, Moses' sister, whose name was Maryam: ﴿Follow him﴾: seek his trace until you know his news. From this comes "qisas" (narrative), because it is a story in which the second follows the first. ﴿So she watched him from afar﴾: she looked at him from a distance, ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that she was his sister. Ibn 'Abbas said: "janb" (distance) means that a person's sight reaches a distant thing while the one who is at his side does not notice him.

Qatadah said: She kept looking at him as if she did not want him, and she was looking at him. Qatadah read "'an janb" with a fatha on the jim and sukun on the nun. Al-Nu'man ibn Salim read "'an janib," meaning "from the direction of."

﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses﴾: "al-maraqi" is the plural of murdi'ah (wet-nurse), ﴿before﴾, i.e., before the coming of Moses' mother. This is because he would be brought one wet-nurse after another, but he would not accept the breast of any woman, which distressed them. When Moses' sister saw what they were doing and how they dealt with him, which his mother had sent her to find out about, she said to them: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will undertake him for you﴾, i.e., will guarantee him, nurse him, and take him into their care? She was a woman whose child had been killed, so the thing most beloved to her was to find a young child and nurse him. ﴿And they are sincere to him.﴾ Sincerity (nush) is the purification of work from any taint of corruption, and it is the opposite of deceit. They said: "Yes." So they brought her, and she went to her mother and informed her of her son's situation, and she came to them with her. When the infant smelled his mother's scent, he took her breast. This is His saying: ﴿So We returned him to his mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve, and that she might know that the promise of God is true, but most of them do not know﴾, meaning that God had promised her to return him to her.

Al-Suddi and Ibn Juraij said: When Moses' sister said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will undertake him for you while they are sincere to him?﴾, they seized her and said: "You know this boy; direct us to his family." She said: "I do not know him, but I only said: they are sincere to the king." 

﴿And when he reached his maturity﴾. Al-Kalbi said: al-ashudd (maturity) is between eighteen and thirty years of age. The other exegetes said: al-ashudd is thirty-three years. ﴿And became mature﴾, i.e., reached forty years.

Abu Muhammad al-Makhladi informed us, saying: Abu al-Wafa' al-Mu'ammal ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Isa informed us, saying:

al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sulaym narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman ibn Khutaym informed me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the saying of God, Glorified be He: ﴿When he reached his maturity and became mature﴾. He said: al-ashudd is thirty-three years, and al-istiwa' is forty years. The lifespan that God set for the son of Adam is sixty years. Then he recited: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough that whoever would be mindful could be mindful therein, and the warner came to you?﴾ [Surat Fatir: 37.]

﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾: understanding and comprehension, ﴿and knowledge.﴾ Mujahid said: It was said: prophethood. ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾

And Moses entered the city — that is, Moses — (Sudi said: the city of Memphis) from the land of Egypt. Others said it was a town called Khanin, two farsakhs from Egypt. [Note the bracketed marginal references in the source are part of the commentary's apparatus.]

And he entered the city "at a time of heedlessness of its people." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: he entered it between sunset and the night prayer. Others said: at midday, at the time of the noon rest. The scholars differed over the reason why Moses entered the city at this time. As-Suddi said: when Moses was commanded, he rode the mounts of Pharaoh and dressed as he dressed, for he was called "Moses, son of Pharaoh." Then Pharaoh rode a mount while Moses was not with him. When Moses came, he was told, "Pharaoh has ridden out," so he rode after him, and the midday rest overtook him in a land called Memphis. He entered it at midday, when its markets had gone quiet and there was no one in its streets. This is what God, glorified is He, means: "And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people."

Ibn Ishaq said: Moses had a following among the Children of Israel who listened to him, followed him and gathered around him. When his opinion grew firm and he knew the truth he was upon, he resolved to part from Pharaoh and his people. He opposed them in their religion, spoke out, showed enmity and denounced them, until mention of this reached them, and they feared him and he feared them, so that he would not enter a town except in fear and concealment. One day he entered it "at a time of heedlessness of its people."

Ibn Zayd said: When Moses, as a child, seized Pharaoh by the beard with his staff, Pharaoh said, "This is our enemy, by whom you slew the Children of Israel." His wife said, "No, he is a child." Then she brought a coal and a jewel; when Moses took the coal and put it in his mouth, it became a knot in his tongue, and Pharaoh abandoned killing him and ordered him expelled from his city. So he did not enter upon them except after he grew up and reached his maturity. "And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people" — concerning Moses — meaning after they had forgotten his news and his affair, because of the long time since they had last seen him.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said, concerning "at a time of heedlessness of its people": it was a day of festivity for them, when they were occupied with their amusement and play.

"And he found in it two men fighting: one of his own party, from his religion, from the Children of Israel, and the other of his enemy, from his opponents, from the Copts." The exegetes said: the one of his party was the Samiri, and the one of his enemy was the cook of Pharaoh, whose name was Fitlyun.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Musa ibn Muhammad told us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Alawiyyah told us, saying: Isma'il ibn Isa told us, saying: al-Musayyib ibn Sharik told us, saying: his name was Fathun and he was Pharaoh's baker; they said he was made to carry firewood to the kitchen. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Moses reached his maturity and became a man, no one of Pharaoh's family could reach any of the Children of Israel with oppression or forced labour in his presence, until they fully resisted. Then one day as he walked in a part of the city, he came upon two men fighting, one of the Children of Israel and the other of Pharaoh's family. The Israelite called on him for help against the Egyptian. Moses grew angry, and his anger intensified because the man had mistreated him, although he knew Moses' standing among the Children of Israel and his protection of them. People knew only that this was because of his nursing by Moses' mother. He said to the Egyptian, "Let him go." The Egyptian said, "He is only taking him to carry firewood to your father's kitchen." The two disputed with each other, and the Egyptian said to Moses, "You have been intent on making me carry it for you."

Moses had been given strength in stature and vigour in power and force, so he struck him with the full of his palm, not intending to kill him. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-wakz is pushing with the fingertips. In the codex of Abdullah it reads "fa-nakazahu" with a nun; wakz, luka, nakz and nakz are one, and their meaning is pushing. "Then he decreed against him," that is, he killed him and finished his affair. Everything you finish, you have "qadaytu" it. A poet said:

"Will they match us, when they have seen their hunter... the lion has bitten him and the bravest has finished him off" — that is, he killed him.

When Moses killed him he regretted his killing and said, "This is from the work of Satan; he is an enemy, a manifest misleader." He said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me," and He forgave him; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. He said, "My Lord, because of what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness, I will never be a supporter to the criminals." Ibn Abbas said: he did not make an exception, and so he was tested. Qatadah said: meaning, I will never again help in a sin.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Khalid told us, saying: Dawud ibn Sulayman told us, saying: Abd ibn Humayd told us, saying: Ubaydullah ibn Musa told us, from Salamah ibn Nubayt, who said: One of the governors, who was Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim, sent to ad-Dahhak with the grants of the people of Bukhara, and said, "Give them to them." He said, "Excuse me." He kept asking to be excused until he was excused. One of his companions said to him, "You take nothing?" He said, "I do not love to help the oppressors in any part of their affairs."

And by the same chain, from Abd Allah, who said: Ya'la told us, saying: Ubaydullah ibn al-Walid al-Wassafi told us, who said: I said to Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "I have a brother who takes up a pen, and he only writes what comes in and what goes out." He said, "If he takes up his pen, that is a livelihood; if he leaves it, he will be in need, debt will fall upon him, and he has dependants." I said, "From the head?" He said, "Khalid ibn Abd Allah." He said, "Do you not read what the righteous servant said: 'My Lord, because of what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter to the criminals'? So let him not help them, for God, exalted is He, will make him independent."

"So he woke in the city, fearful, from the killing of the Copt, lest he be seized and slain for it, awaiting news. Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was calling him for help, asking him to aid him. The root of this is from al-sarakh (outcry), as one says, 'O such-and-such of the tribe!'"

Ibn Abbas said: Someone went to Pharaoh and said to him, "The Children of Israel have killed a man of ours; take our right for us and do not give them any concession in this." He said, "Seek for me his killer and one who will testify against him, for it is not right to judge without proof or evidence; so search for that." While they were going about and finding no evidence, Moses passed the next day and saw that Israelite fighting another Egyptian who wanted to press him into forced labour. The Israelite called on Moses for help against the Egyptian. He met Moses, who regretted what he had done the day before in killing the Copt. Moses said to the Israelite, "Indeed you are an manifest one in error, clearly misguided: yesterday you fought a man and killed him because of you, and today you fight another and call on me against him."

It was said: he only said to the Egyptian, "Indeed you are a manifest one in error," because of your oppression and your wrongdoing. The first view is more correct and more fitting to the arrangement of the verse.

Ibn Abbas said: Then Moses stretched out his hand, intending to seize the Egyptian. The Israelite looked at Moses after he had said to him, "Indeed you are a manifest one in error," and behold, he was angry, as his anger had been the day before; so he feared that after he had said that to him, Moses meant to attack him. But Moses had not meant him; he had meant the Egyptian. So he said, "O Moses, do you want to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land, by killing unjustly." Akrimah and al-Sha'bi said: a person is not a tyrant until he kills two souls without right.

"And you do not want to be among the reformers." Then the two parted. When the Copt heard what the Israelite said, he knew that Moses had killed that Egyptian, so he went off to Pharaoh and informed him of it. Pharaoh ordered Moses' killing, and no one had been found responsible for the Copt's killing until Moses' companion said what he said.

Ibn Abbas said: When Pharaoh sent the executioners to kill Moses, they took the main road. A man from the party of Moses came from the farthest part of the city, that is, its end, and took a short route, outpacing them, and warned him, until he took another road. That is His saying: "And a man came..." They differed about him. Most people of interpretation said: he was Hizqil ibn Subaru, the believer of Pharaoh's family, who was Pharaoh's cousin. Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i said: his name was Shim'un; it was also said: Sim'an.

"From the farthest part of the city, running." Al-Kalbi said: he hastened in his walk to warn him. Muqatil said: he walked on his feet. "He said, 'O Moses, the chiefs are conferring about you to kill you,'" that is, they intend to kill you and deliberate about you. It was also said: they command one another to it, like His saying: "And confer among yourselves in kindness." Al-Nimr ibn Taghlib said:

"I see people have made a custom, and in every new matter they confer."

"So leave this city; indeed I am to you one of the sincere advisers." Moses left it, fearful, watching, awaiting pursuit. He said, "My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people." When he turned toward Madyan, that is, headed for it and aimed at it, passing beyond Pharaoh's authority — it is said: his house is opposite the house of so-and-so when they face each other; it comes from "liqa'" (meeting). Madyan is not declined, because it is the name of a known town. The poet said:

"The monks of Madyan, if they saw you, would descend, and the mountain goats from the bewilderment of the wise..."

It is named after Madyan ibn Ibrahim, and the town was named after him, as the cities of Madaʼin were named after his brother Madaʼin ibn Ibrahim. He said, "It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right path." He meant the road to Madyan, and he said this because he did not know the way to it. When he prayed, an angel on a horse, holding a staff, came to him and led him to Madyan.

The exegetes said: Moses left Egypt without provision, dirham, mount or shoes, for Madyan, which was eight nights' journey apart — roughly from Kufa to Basra. He had no food except the leaves of trees. Ibn Jubayr said: he left Egypt barefoot, and by the time he reached Madyan the soles of his feet had worn away.

And he entered the city "at a time of heedlessness of its people." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: he entered it between sunset and the night prayer. Others said: at midday, at the time of the noon rest. The scholars differed over the reason why Moses entered the city at this time. As-Suddi said: when Moses was commanded, he rode the mounts of Pharaoh and dressed as he dressed, for he was called "Moses, son of Pharaoh." Then Pharaoh rode a mount while Moses was not with him. When Moses came, he was told, "Pharaoh has ridden out," so he rode after him, and the midday rest overtook him in a land called Memphis. He entered it at midday, when its markets had gone quiet and there was no one in its streets. This is what God, glorified is He, means: "And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people."

Ibn Ishaq said: Moses had a following among the Children of Israel who listened to him, followed him and gathered around him. When his opinion grew firm and he knew the truth he was upon, he resolved to part from Pharaoh and his people. He opposed them in their religion, spoke out, showed enmity and denounced them, until mention of this reached them, and they feared him and he feared them, so that he would not enter a town except in fear and concealment. One day he entered it "at a time of heedlessness of its people."

Ibn Zayd said: When Moses, as a child, seized Pharaoh by the beard with his staff, Pharaoh said, "This is our enemy, by whom you slew the Children of Israel." His wife said, "No, he is a child." Then she brought a coal and a jewel; when Moses took the coal and put it in his mouth, it became a knot in his tongue, and Pharaoh abandoned killing him and ordered him expelled from his city. So he did not enter upon them except after he grew up and reached his maturity. "And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people" — concerning Moses — meaning after they had forgotten his news and his affair, because of the long time since they had last seen him.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said, concerning "at a time of heedlessness of its people": it was a day of festivity for them, when they were occupied with their amusement and play.

"And he found in it two men fighting: one of his own party, from his religion, from the Children of Israel, and the other of his enemy, from his opponents, from the Copts." The exegetes said: the one of his party was the Samiri, and the one of his enemy was the cook of Pharaoh, whose name was Fitlyun.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Musa ibn Muhammad told us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Alawiyyah told us, saying: Isma'il ibn Isa told us, saying: al-Musayyib ibn Sharik told us, saying: his name was Fathun and he was Pharaoh's baker; they said he was made to carry firewood to the kitchen. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Moses reached his maturity and became a man, no one of Pharaoh's family could reach any of the Children of Israel with oppression or forced labour in his presence, until they fully resisted. Then one day as he walked in a part of the city, he came upon two men fighting, one of the Children of Israel and the other of Pharaoh's family. The Israelite called on him for help against the Egyptian. Moses grew angry, and his anger intensified because the man had mistreated him, although he knew Moses' standing among the Children of Israel and his protection of them. People knew only that this was because of his nursing by Moses' mother. He said to the Egyptian, "Let him go." The Egyptian said, "He is only taking him to carry firewood to your father's kitchen." The two disputed with each other, and the Egyptian said to Moses, "You have been intent on making me carry it for you."

Moses had been given strength in stature and vigour in power and force, so he struck him with the full of his palm, not intending to kill him. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-wakz is pushing with the fingertips. In the codex of Abdullah it reads "fa-nakazahu" with a nun; wakz, luka, nakz and nakz are one, and their meaning is pushing. "Then he decreed against him," that is, he killed him and finished his affair. Everything you finish, you have "qadaytu" it. A poet said:

"Will they match us, when they have seen their hunter... the lion has bitten him and the bravest has finished him off" — that is, he killed him.

When Moses killed him he regretted his killing and said, "This is from the work of Satan; he is an enemy, a manifest misleader." He said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me," and He forgave him; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. He said, "My Lord, because of what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness, I will never be a supporter to the criminals." Ibn Abbas said: he did not make an exception, and so he was tested. Qatadah said: meaning, I will never again help in a sin.

Abdullah ibn Hamid informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Khalid told us, saying: Dawud ibn Sulayman told us, saying: Abd ibn Humayd told us, saying: Ubaydullah ibn Musa told us, from Salamah ibn Nubayt, who said: One of the governors, who was Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim, sent to ad-Dahhak with the grants of the people of Bukhara, and said, "Give them to them." He said, "Excuse me." He kept asking to be excused until he was excused. One of his companions said to him, "You take nothing?" He said, "I do not love to help the oppressors in any part of their affairs."

And by the same chain, from Abd Allah, who said: Ya'la told us, saying: Ubaydullah ibn al-Walid al-Wassafi told us, who said: I said to Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "I have a brother who takes up a pen, and he only writes what comes in and what goes out." He said, "If he takes up his pen, that is a livelihood; if he leaves it, he will be in need, debt will fall upon him, and he has dependants." I said, "From the head?" He said, "Khalid ibn Abd Allah." He said, "Do you not read what the righteous servant said: 'My Lord, because of what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter to the criminals'? So let him not help them, for God, exalted is He, will make him independent."

Moses said to the Israelite, "Indeed you are an manifest one in error, clearly misguided: yesterday you fought a man and killed him because of you, and today you fight another and call on me against him."

It was said: he only said to the Egyptian, "Indeed you are a manifest one in error," because of your oppression and your wrongdoing. The first view is more correct and more fitting to the arrangement of the verse.

Akrimah and al-Sha'bi said: a person is not a tyrant until he kills two souls without right.

﴿وَلَمَّا وَرَدَ مَاءَ مَدْيَنَ﴾ [When he arrived at the water of Madyan], which was a well belonging to them, ﴿وَجَدَ عَلَيْهِ أُمَّةً مِنَ النَّاسِ يَسْقُونَ﴾ [he found on it a group of people watering], ﴿مَوَاشِيَهُمْ﴾ [their livestock], ﴿وَوَجَدَ مِنْ دُونِهِمُ امْرَأَتَيْنِ تَذُودَانِ﴾ [and he found, apart from them, two women holding back], that is, detaining and preventing their sheep from straying and running off. Al-Hasan said: they were restraining [their sheep] from mixing with the sheep of the people, and the mention of the sheep was omitted for brevity. Qatadah said: [they were holding back] the people from their ewes. Abu Malik and Ibn Ishaq said: they were holding back their flock from the water until the livestock of the people had departed and left the well free for them; then they would water their flock, because of their weakness. [In the Isfahan manuscript: tasqiyan.] This view is more correct because of what follows it, which is His saying:

﴿قَالَ مَا خَطْبُكُمَا﴾ [He said: what is your affair?], that is, Musa said: what is your situation, that you do not water your livestock together with the people?

﴿قَالَتَا لَا نَسْقِي حَتَّى يُصْدِرَ الرِّعَاءُ﴾ [They said: we do not water until the shepherds depart]. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Ja'far and Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil read it with a fathah on the ya' and a dammah on the dal (يَصْدُرَ), making the verb refer to the shepherds, meaning until they return from the water. The others read it with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the dal (يُصْدِرَ), meaning until they turn their livestock away from the water. Al-Ru'a' is the plural of ra'in, like tajir and tujjar. The meaning of the verse is: we do not water our livestock until the shepherds have departed, because we cannot bear to water them and we cannot compete with the men; when they have departed, we water our livestock with what remains of their water in the trough.

﴿وَأَبُونَا شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ﴾ [And our father is an elderly old man], who cannot water his livestock. They differed about the name of their father. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and al-Hasan said: he was Shu'ayb the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and upon all the prophets, whose name was Shu'ayb ibn Yuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim. Wahb, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu 'Ubaydah ibn 'Abd Allah said: he was Bathrun, the nephew of Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb had died before that, after his sight had failed; he was buried between the Maqam and Zamzam.

Hammad ibn Salamah narrated, from Abu Hamzah al-Dab'i, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the name of the father of Musa's wife, the man of Madyan, was Bathra. They said: when Musa (peace be upon him) heard their words, he had mercy on them, and he uprooted a rock from the top of another well that was near them, which a group of people could not lift. Shurayh said: ten men could not lift it. It was also said that he pushed the people away from the water, took their bucket, and watered their flock. This is narrated from Ibn Ishaq, and it is the meaning of His saying, glory be to Him:

﴿فَسَقَى لَهُمَا ثُمَّ تَوَلَّى إِلَى الظِّلِّ﴾ [So he watered [their flock] for them, then he withdrew to the shade]. Al-Suddi said: the shade of a tree. 'Umar ibn Maymun narrated from 'Abd Allah, who said: I travelled on a camel of mine for two nights until I reached Madyan in the morning. I asked about the tree to which Musa had retreated, and there was a green tree that was lush; my camel was drawn to it, and it was hungry, so it took hold of it and tugged at it for a while, but did not uproot it. So I invoked Allah, glory be to Him, on behalf of Musa, and then I departed. [In the Isfahan manuscript: yu'alijuha.] [In the Isfahan manuscript: then he uprooted it, lam (not) yaqta'ha.]

﴿فَقَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي لِمَا أَنْزَلْتَ إِلَيَّ مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ﴾ [He said: My Lord, indeed I am in need of whatever good You send down to me]. Qutrub said: the lam here means "to" (ila). The Arabs say: ihtajtu lahu and ihtajtu ilayhi, with the same meaning. Min khayrin means food. Faqir means in need. Ibn 'Abbas said: he said this while the greenness of the herbs was visible in his belly from emaciation; he asked Allah for nothing except that he eat. Al-Baqir said: he said it while he was in need of half a date.

They said: when the two women returned quickly to their father, before the other people, and their flocks were full and well-fed, he said to them: what has hastened you? They said: we found a righteous man, who had mercy on us, and he watered our flock before the people. So he said to one of them: go and call him for me.

﴿فَجَاءَتْهُ إِحْدَاهُمَا تَمْشِي عَلَى اسْتِحْيَاءٍ﴾ [So one of them came to him walking with shyness]. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: she was concealed, her garment wrapped around her, and she had covered her face with her hand. Qatadah narrated from Mutarrif, who said: By Allah, if the Prophet of Allah had anything, he would not have followed her, but necessity compelled him to that.

﴿قَالَتْ إِنَّ أَبِي يَدْعُوكَ لِيَجْزِيَكَ أَجْرَ مَا سَقَيْتَ لَنَا﴾ [She said: indeed my father invites you so that he may reward you for what you watered for us]. So Musa went with her, following her. The wind blew and pressed the woman's garment against her buttocks, so Musa disliked to see that from her, and he said to her: walk behind me, and direct me to the way, and guide me to it if I go astray, for we are the children of Ya'qub and we do not look at the backsides of women.

﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُ﴾ [When he came to him], that is, the old man, ﴿وَقَصَّ عَلَيْهِ الْقَصَصَ﴾ [and he related to him the narrative], that is, he informed him of his affair and the reason that had driven him out of his land, ﴿قَالَ لَا تَخَفْ﴾ [he said: do not fear], ﴿نَجَوْتَ مِنَ الْقَوْمِ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ [you have escaped from the wrongdoing people], meaning Pharaoh and his people, who have no authority in our land.

﴿قَالَتْ إِحْدَاهُمَا﴾ [One of them said], and she was the one whom Musa later married: ﴿يَا أَبَتِ اسْتَأْجِرْهُ﴾ [O father, hire him], ﴿لِرَعْيِ أَغْنَامِنَا﴾ [to pasture our sheep], ﴿إِنَّ خَيْرَ مَنِ اسْتَأْجَرْتَ الْقَوِيُّ الْأَمِينُ﴾ [indeed the best one you could hire is the strong, the trustworthy]. Her father said to her: and what makes you know of his strength and trustworthiness? She said: as for his strength, when he saw us holding back our sheep from the water, he said to us: is there a well near you? We said: yes, but over it is a rock that only forty men can lift. He said: take me to it, and he took the rock with his hand and moved it aside.

As for his trustworthiness, he said to me on the way: walk behind me, and if I go astray, throw a pebble in front of me, until I am guided by its direction. [In the Isfahan manuscript: nahjan.]

At that, the old man said to Musa: ﴿إِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُنْكِحَكَ إِحْدَى ابْنَتَيَّ هَاتَيْنِ﴾ [Indeed I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine], and their names were Safurah and Layya. This is the saying of Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i, who said: the wife of Musa was Safurah. Ibn Ishaq said: Safurah and Sharfa. Others said: the elder was Safra and the younger Safir. ﴿عَلَى أَنْ تَأْجُرَنِي﴾ [on condition that you serve me], meaning: hire yourself to me. The scholars said: on condition that you repay me, by the marriage, by pasturing my livestock ﴿ثَمَانِيَ حِجَجٍ﴾ [for eight years], each year being a hijjah (year). He made that her dowry. He said: the Arabs say: ajarakal-lah, meaning he rewards you, that is, he compensates you. ﴿فَإِنْ أَتْمَمْتَ عَشْراً﴾ [And if you complete ten], that is, ten years, ﴿فَمِنْ عِنْدِكَ﴾ [then it is from you], and you are then generous and bountiful, and it is not something he stipulated upon you in the marriage contract. ﴿وَمَا أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَشُقَّ عَلَيْكَ﴾ [And I do not wish to burden you], ﴿سَتَجِدُنِي إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ﴾ [you will find me, God willing, among the righteous], meaning among those who fulfil their covenant and treat their companions well. He said: ﴿ذَلِكَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ أَيَّمَا الْأَجَلَيْنِ قَضَيْتُ﴾ [That is between me and you; whichever of the two terms I fulfil], the eight or the ten, ﴿فَلَا عُدْوَانَ عَلَيَّ﴾ [there shall be no injustice against me], ﴿وَاللَّهُ عَلَى مَا نَقُولُ وَكِيلٌ﴾ [and Allah is Witness over what we say], meaning Guardian and Observer.

The scholars of the reports of the prophets said: when Musa and his companion (peace be upon them both) concluded this contract between them, his father-in-law ordered one of his two daughters to give Musa a staff with which he could drive off predators from his sheep. They differed about the nature of that staff. 'Ikrimah said: Adam brought it out of Paradise, and Jibril took it after the death of Adam, and it remained with him until he met Musa at night and handed it to him. Others said: the prophets continued to inherit it until it reached Shu'ayb, and the staffs of the prophets were with him, and he gave it to Musa.

Al-Suddi said: that staff had been entrusted to him by an angel in the form of a man, and he ordered his daughter to bring him a staff. The girl entered and took the staff and brought it to him. When the old man saw it, he said to his daughter: bring him another. When she threw it and tried to take another, it would not fall into her hand except that one, and each time it flew into her hand, until she had done this several times. So he gave it to Musa, and Musa took it with him. Then the old man regretted it and said: it was a deposit. So he went out to meet Musa, and when he met him he said: give me the staff. Musa said: it is my staff. He refused to give it to him, and they disputed until they agreed to take as judge the first man who came upon them. Then an angel came walking, and he judged between them, and said: place it on the ground; whoever lifts it, it belongs to him. The old man tried to lift it but could not, and Musa took it in his hand and lifted it, and the old man left it to him.

Hayyan narrated from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: in the house of Bathrun there was a room that no one entered except Bathrun and his daughter who was married to Musa; she used to sweep it and clean it. In the room there were thirteen staffs, and Bathrun had eleven sons. Whenever one of them reached maturity, he ordered him to enter the room and take out one of those staffs, but the son would burn until all of them died. Then Musa returned one day to his home and did not find his family, and he needed a staff for his herding; so he entered that room, took one of those staffs, and went out with it. When his wife learned of that, she went to her father and told him. Bathrun was pleased and said to her: this husband of yours is a prophet, and this staff has a great matter with it.

It is also reported in some accounts that when Musa (peace be upon him) rose the next morning after the contract and wished to pasture, his father-in-law Shu'ayb said to him: take these sheep, and when you reach the fork in the road, take the left and not the right, even if the pasture there is more abundant, for there is a huge serpent there, and I fear for you and for the sheep from it. So Musa went with the sheep, and when he reached the fork in the road, the sheep took the right; Musa struggled to turn them towards the left, but they did not obey him, so Musa followed their track. He saw grass and lush greenery the like of which he had never seen, and he did not see the serpent. Musa slept while the sheep grazed, and suddenly the serpent came; the staff of Musa rose up and fought it until it killed it, and then returned to Musa's side, and it was bloodied.

When Musa awoke, he saw the staff bloodied and the serpent killed. He was delighted at that and knew that Allah, glory be to Him, had power and will in that staff. He returned to Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb was blind; he touched the sheep, and they were in a better condition than they had been. He asked him, and Musa told him the story. Shu'ayb rejoiced at that and knew that Musa and his staff had a great matter. Shu'ayb wished to reward Musa for his good pasturing, out of honour for him and as a kindness to his daughter, and he said to him: I have given you from the kids that my sheep will bear this year, every spotted and white-spotted one. Then Allah, exalted, revealed to Musa: strike the water in the trough of the sheep with your staff.

He said: Musa struck the water with his staff and then watered the sheep from it, and not one of them failed to give birth, each bearing its young between spotted and white-spotted. Shu'ayb knew that this was a provision that Allah had brought to Musa and his wife, so he fulfilled his condition to him and handed over the sheep to him.

Qatadah said: [they were holding back] the people from their ewes. He said: take me to it, and he took the rock with his hand and moved it aside.

When the old man saw it, he said to his daughter: bring him another. When she threw it and tried to take another, it would not fall into her hand except that one, and each time it flew into her hand, until she had done this several times. So he gave it to Musa, and Musa took it with him. Then the old man regretted it and said: it was a deposit. So he went out to meet Musa, and when he met him he said: give me the staff. Musa said: it is my staff. He refused to give it to him, and they disputed until they agreed to take as judge the first man who came upon them. Then an angel came walking, and he judged between them, and said: place it on the ground; whoever lifts it, it belongs to him. The old man tried to lift it but could not, and Musa took it in his hand and lifted it, and the old man left it to him.

Hayyan narrated from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: in the house of Bathrun there was a room that no one entered except Bathrun and his daughter who was married to Musa; she used to sweep it and clean it. In the room there were thirteen staffs, and Bathrun had eleven sons. Whenever one of them reached maturity, he ordered him to enter the room and take out one of those staffs, but the son would burn until all of them died. Then Musa returned one day to his home and did not find his family, and he needed a staff for his herding; so he entered that room, took one of those staffs, and went out with it. When his wife learned of that, she went to her father and told him. Bathrun was pleased and said to her: this husband of yours is a prophet, and this staff has a great matter with it.

It is also reported in some accounts that when Musa (peace be upon him) rose the next morning after the contract and wished to pasture, his father-in-law Shu'ayb said to him: take these sheep, and when you reach the fork in the road, take the left and not the right, even if the pasture there is more abundant, for there is a huge serpent there, and I fear for you and for the sheep from it. So Musa went with the sheep, and when he reached the fork in the road, the sheep took the right; Musa struggled to turn them towards the left, but they did not obey him, so Musa followed their track. He saw grass and lush greenery the like of which he had never seen, and he did not see the serpent. Musa slept while the sheep grazed, and suddenly the serpent came; the staff of Musa rose up and fought it until it killed it, and then returned to Musa's side, and it was bloodied.

When Musa awoke, he saw the staff bloodied and the serpent killed. He was delighted at that and knew that Allah, glory be to Him, had power and will in that staff. He returned to Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb was blind; he touched the sheep, and they were in a better condition than they had been. He asked him, and Musa told him the story. Shu'ayb rejoiced at that and knew that Musa and his staff had a great matter. Shu'ayb wished to reward Musa for his good pasturing, out of honour for him and as a kindness to his daughter, and he said to him: I have given you from the kids that my sheep will bear this year, every spotted and white-spotted one. Then Allah, exalted, revealed to Musa: strike the water in the trough of the sheep with your staff.

He said: ﴿ذَلِكَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ أَيَّمَا الْأَجَلَيْنِ قَضَيْتُ﴾ [That is between me and you; whichever of the two terms I fulfil], the eight or the ten, ﴿فَلَا عُدْوَانَ عَلَيَّ﴾ [there shall be no injustice against me], ﴿وَاللَّهُ عَلَى مَا نَقُولُ وَكِيلٌ﴾ [and Allah is Witness over what we say], meaning Guardian and Observer.

The scholars said: on condition that you repay me, by the marriage, by pasturing my livestock ﴿ثَمَانِيَ حِجَجٍ﴾ [for eight years], each year being a hijjah (year). He made that her dowry. He said: the Arabs say: ajarakal-lah, meaning he rewards you, that is, he compensates you. ﴿فَإِنْ أَتْمَمْتَ عَشْراً﴾ [And if you complete ten], that is, ten years, ﴿فَمِنْ عِنْدِكَ﴾ [then it is from you], and you are then generous and bountiful, and it is not something he stipulated upon you in the marriage contract. ﴿وَمَا أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَشُقَّ عَلَيْكَ﴾ [And I do not wish to burden you], ﴿سَتَجِدُنِي إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ﴾ [you will find me, God willing, among the righteous], meaning among those who fulfil their covenant and treat their companions well. He said: ﴿ذَلِكَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ أَيَّمَا الْأَجَلَيْنِ قَضَيْتُ﴾ [That is between me and you; whichever of the two terms I fulfil], the eight or the ten, ﴿فَلَا عُدْوَانَ عَلَيَّ﴾ [there shall be no injustice against me], ﴿وَاللَّهُ عَلَى مَا نَقُولُ وَكِيلٌ﴾ [and Allah is Witness over what we say], meaning Guardian and Observer.

The scholars of the reports of the prophets said: when Musa and his companion (peace be upon them both) concluded this contract between them, his father-in-law ordered one of his two daughters to give Musa a staff with which he could drive off predators from his sheep. They differed about the nature of that staff. 'Ikrimah said: Adam brought it out of Paradise, and Jibril took it after the death of Adam, and it remained with him until he met Musa at night and handed it to him. Others said: the prophets continued to inherit it until it reached Shu'ayb, and the staffs of the prophets were with him, and he gave it to Musa.

Al-Suddi said: that staff had been entrusted to him by an angel in the form of a man, and he ordered his daughter to bring him a staff. The girl entered and took the staff and brought it to him. When the old man saw it, he said to his daughter: bring him another. When she threw it and tried to take another, it would not fall into her hand except that one, and each time it flew into her hand, until she had done this several times. So he gave it to Musa, and Musa took it with him. Then the old man regretted it and said: it was a deposit. So he went out to meet Musa, and when he met him he said: give me the staff. Musa said: it is my staff. He refused to give it to him, and they disputed until they agreed to take as judge the first man who came upon them. Then an angel came walking, and he judged between them, and said: place it on the ground; whoever lifts it, it belongs to him. The old man tried to lift it but could not, and Musa took it in his hand and lifted it, and the old man left it to him.

Hayyan narrated from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: in the house of Bathrun there was a room that no one entered except Bathrun and his daughter who was married to Musa; she used to sweep it and clean it. In the room there were thirteen staffs, and Bathrun had eleven sons. Whenever one of them reached maturity, he ordered him to enter the room and take out one of those staffs, but the son would burn until all of them died. Then Musa returned one day to his home and did not find his family, and he needed a staff for his herding; so he entered that room, took one of those staffs, and went out with it. When his wife learned of that, she went to her father and told him. Bathrun was pleased and said to her: this husband of yours is a prophet, and this staff has a great matter with it.

It is also reported in some accounts that when Musa (peace be upon him) rose the next morning after the contract and wished to pasture, his father-in-law Shu'ayb said to him: take these sheep, and when you reach the fork in the road, take the left and not the right, even if the pasture there is more abundant, for there is a huge serpent there, and I fear for you and for the sheep from it. So Musa went with the sheep, and when he reached the fork in the road, the sheep took the right; Musa struggled to turn them towards the left, but they did not obey him, so Musa followed their track. He saw grass and lush greenery the like of which he had never seen, and he did not see the serpent. Musa slept while the sheep grazed, and suddenly the serpent came; the staff of Musa rose up and fought it until it killed it, and then returned to Musa's side, and it was bloodied.

When Musa awoke, he saw the staff bloodied and the serpent killed. He was delighted at that and knew that Allah, glory be to Him, had power and will in that staff. He returned to Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb was blind; he touched the sheep, and they were in a better condition than they had been. He asked him, and Musa told him the story. Shu'ayb rejoiced at that and knew that Musa and his staff had a great matter. Shu'ayb wished to reward Musa for his good pasturing, out of honour for him and as a kindness to his daughter, and he said to him: I have given you from the kids that my sheep will bear this year, every spotted and white-spotted one. Then Allah, exalted, revealed to Musa: strike the water in the trough of the sheep with your staff.

He said: Musa struck the water with his staff and then watered the sheep from it, and not one of them failed to give birth, each bearing its young between spotted and white-spotted. Shu'ayb knew that this was a provision that Allah had brought to Musa and his wife, so he fulfilled his condition to him and handed over the sheep to him.

﴿وَلَمَّا وَرَدَ مَاءَ مَدْيَنَ﴾ [When he arrived at the water of Madyan], which was a well belonging to them, ﴿وَجَدَ عَلَيْهِ أُمَّةً مِنَ النَّاسِ يَسْقُونَ﴾ [he found on it a group of people watering], ﴿مَوَاشِيَهُمْ﴾ [their livestock], ﴿وَوَجَدَ مِنْ دُونِهِمُ امْرَأَتَيْنِ تَذُودَانِ﴾ [and he found, apart from them, two women holding back], that is, detaining and preventing their sheep from straying and running off. Al-Hasan said: they were restraining [their sheep] from mixing with the sheep of the people, and the mention of the sheep was omitted for brevity. Qatadah said: [they were holding back] the people from their ewes. Abu Malik and Ibn Ishaq said: they were holding back their flock from the water until the livestock of the people had departed and left the well free for them; then they would water their flock, because of their weakness. [In the Isfahan manuscript: tasqiyan.] This view is more correct because of what follows it, which is His saying:

﴿قَالَ مَا خَطْبُكُمَا﴾ [He said: what is your affair?], that is, Musa said: what is your situation, that you do not water your livestock together with the people?

﴿قَالَتَا لَا نَسْقِي حَتَّى يُصْدِرَ الرِّعَاءُ﴾ [They said: we do not water until the shepherds depart]. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Ja'far and Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil read it with a fathah on the ya' and a dammah on the dal (يَصْدُرَ), making the verb refer to the shepherds, meaning until they return from the water. The others read it with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the dal (يُصْدِرَ), meaning until they turn their livestock away from the water. Al-Ru'a' is the plural of ra'in, like tajir and tujjar. The meaning of the verse is: we do not water our livestock until the shepherds have departed, because we cannot bear to water them and we cannot compete with the men; when they have departed, we water our livestock with what remains of their water in the trough.

﴿وَأَبُونَا شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ﴾ [And our father is an elderly old man], who cannot water his livestock. They differed about the name of their father. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and al-Hasan said: he was Shu'ayb the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and upon all the prophets, whose name was Shu'ayb ibn Yuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim. Wahb, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu 'Ubaydah ibn 'Abd Allah said: he was Bathrun, the nephew of Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb had died before that, after his sight had failed; he was buried between the Maqam and Zamzam.

Hammad ibn Salamah narrated, from Abu Hamzah al-Dab'i, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the name of the father of Musa's wife, the man of Madyan, was Bathra. They said: when Musa (peace be upon him) heard their words, he had mercy on them, and he uprooted a rock from the top of another well that was near them, which a group of people could not lift. Shurayh said: ten men could not lift it. It was also said that he pushed the people away from the water, took their bucket, and watered their flock. This is narrated from Ibn Ishaq, and it is the meaning of His saying, glory be to Him:

﴿فَسَقَى لَهُمَا ثُمَّ تَوَلَّى إِلَى الظِّلِّ﴾ [So he watered [their flock] for them, then he withdrew to the shade]. Al-Suddi said: the shade of a tree. 'Umar ibn Maymun narrated from 'Abd Allah, who said: I travelled on a camel of mine for two nights until I reached Madyan in the morning. I asked about the tree to which Musa had retreated, and there was a green tree that was lush; my camel was drawn to it, and it was hungry, so it took hold of it and tugged at it for a while, but did not uproot it. So I invoked Allah, glory be to Him, on behalf of Musa, and then I departed. [In the Isfahan manuscript: yu'alijuha.] [In the Isfahan manuscript: then he uprooted it, lam (not) yaqta'ha.]

﴿فَقَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي لِمَا أَنْزَلْتَ إِلَيَّ مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ﴾ [He said: My Lord, indeed I am in need of whatever good You send down to me]. Qutrub said: the lam here means "to" (ila). The Arabs say: ihtajtu lahu and ihtajtu ilayhi, with the same meaning. Min khayrin means food. Faqir means in need. Ibn 'Abbas said: he said this while the greenness of the herbs was visible in his belly from emaciation; he asked Allah for nothing except that he eat. Al-Baqir said: he said it while he was in need of half a date.

They said: when the two women returned quickly to their father, before the other people, and their flocks were full and well-fed, he said to them: what has hastened you? They said: we found a righteous man, who had mercy on us, and he watered our flock before the people. So he said to one of them: go and call him for me.

﴿فَجَاءَتْهُ إِحْدَاهُمَا تَمْشِي عَلَى اسْتِحْيَاءٍ﴾ [So one of them came to him walking with shyness]. Qatadah narrated from Mutarrif, who said: By Allah, if the Prophet of Allah had anything, he would not have followed her, but necessity compelled him to that.

So Musa went with her, following her. The wind blew and pressed the woman's garment against her buttocks, so Musa disliked to see that from her, and he said to her: walk behind me, and direct me to the way, and guide me to it if I go astray, for we are the children of Ya'qub and we do not look at the backsides of women.

﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُ﴾ [When he came to him], that is, the old man, ﴿وَقَصَّ عَلَيْهِ الْقَصَصَ﴾ [and he related to him the narrative], that is, he informed him of his affair and the reason that had driven him out of his land, ﴿قَالَ لَا تَخَفْ﴾ [he said: do not fear], ﴿نَجَوْتَ مِنَ الْقَوْمِ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ [you have escaped from the wrongdoing people], meaning Pharaoh and his people, who have no authority in our land.

﴿قَالَتْ إِحْدَاهُمَا﴾ [One of them said], and she was the one whom Musa later married: ﴿يَا أَبَتِ اسْتَأْجِرْهُ﴾ [O father, hire him], ﴿لِرَعْيِ أَغْنَامِنَا﴾ [to pasture our sheep], ﴿إِنَّ خَيْرَ مَنِ اسْتَأْجَرْتَ الْقَوِيُّ الْأَمِينُ﴾ [indeed the best one you could hire is the strong, the trustworthy]. Her father said to her: and what makes you know of his strength and trustworthiness? She said: as for his strength, when he saw us holding back our sheep from the water, he said to us: is there a well near you? We said: yes, but over it is a rock that only forty men can lift. He said: take me to it, and he took the rock with his hand and moved it aside.

As for his trustworthiness, he said to me on the way: walk behind me, and if I go astray, throw a pebble in front of me, until I am guided by its direction. [In the Isfahan manuscript: nahjan.]

At that, the old man said to Musa: ﴿إِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُنْكِحَكَ إِحْدَى ابْنَتَيَّ هَاتَيْنِ﴾ [Indeed I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine], and their names were Safurah and Layya. This is the saying of Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i, who said: the wife of Musa was Safurah. Ibn Ishaq said: Safurah and Sharfa. Others said: the elder was Safra and the younger Safir. ﴿عَلَى أَنْ تَأْجُرَنِي﴾ [on condition that you serve me], meaning: hire yourself to me. Commentary of al-Tha'alabi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 28, verses 29–35:

﴿Then when Musa had fulfilled the term﴾, i.e., completed it and finished with it.

Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Hamdun informed us, saying: Makki ibn 'Abdan informed us, from 'Abd al-Rahman, who said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Bishr narrated to us, saying: Musa ibn 'Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Aban narrated to us, saying: 'Ikrimah narrated to me, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "Which of the two terms did Musa fulfill?" He said: "The more distant of them and the best of them" [127] [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 5/127.]].

And 'Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muzani informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar al-Hamadhani narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: Ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, from al-Harith [[In the Isfahan manuscript: al-Harth.]] ibn Zayd, from 'Ali ibn Rabah [[In the Isfahan manuscript: Riyah.]], from 'Utbah ibn al-Tayyib, who was one of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), resided in Syria, and died during the time of 'Abd al-Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "Which of the two terms did Musa fulfill?" He said: "The more righteous of them and the most complete of them" [128] [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 5/127.]].

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Hakam ibn Jubayr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: A Jew in Kufa said to me while I was preparing for the Hajj: "I see you as a man who seeks knowledge. Tell me, which of the two terms did Musa fulfill?" I said: "I do not know, but I am now going to the scholar of the Arabs, meaning Ibn 'Abbas, and I will ask him about it." When I arrived in Makkah, I asked Ibn 'Abbas about it, and he said: "He fulfilled the greater of them and the best of them, for when the Prophet promises, he does not break it." Sa'id said: "I went to Iraq, met the Jew and informed him, and he said: 'He spoke the truth. This was not revealed to Musa, and by Allah, the One who knows.'" Wahb said: "He married him to the elder daughter."

It has also been narrated that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "He married the younger of the two and fulfilled the more complete of them" [129] [[Fath al-Qadir: 4/171; Tafsir al-Tabari: 20/85; Tafsir Sufyan al-Thawri: 233.]]. If this report is sound, then there is no deviation from it.

Mujahid said: When Musa had fulfilled the term and remained after that with his father-in-law for ten more years, so he stayed with him for twenty years. Then he asked his permission to return to Egypt to visit his mother and his brother, and he granted him leave. So he set out with his family and property. It was the winter season, and he took a route other than the usual road, fearing the kings of Syria. His wife was in the final stage of pregnancy and he did not know whether she would give birth at night or by day. He traveled in the wilderness, not knowing its paths, and the journey led him to the western side of Mount Sinai, on its right, on a dark night [[In the Isfahan manuscript: cold.]] of severe cold. His wife was seized by labor pains, so he struck a firestarter but it did not produce a spark [the firestarter gave nothing] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 11/171.]]. ﴿He saw a fire from the side of the mount. He said to his family, "Wait, indeed I have seen a fire. Perhaps I will bring you from it some news, or a burning brand from the fire, that you may warm yourselves."﴾ There are three readings of "jadhwah" (a brand): with a fatha on the jim, which is the reading of 'Asim; with a damma, which is the reading of Hamzah; and with a kasra, which is the reading of the rest. Qatadah and Muqatil said: al-Jadhwah is a piece of wood that has partly burned, its plural being judhiyy. Ibn Muqbil said:

"The gatherers of wood for Layla spent the night seeking for her firm, burned logs, neither brittle nor smoldering." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 13/281. Al-Khuwar here means a stick that snaps; al-Mudda'ar is one which, when placed on the fire, does not kindle but smokes.]]

﴿That you may warm yourselves﴾, i.e., that you may get warm and be heated by it against the cold. ﴿Then when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree﴾, i.e., from the direction of the tree, on the right of Musa. Aslam al-'Aqili read "fi al-buq'ah" with a fatha on the ba'. ﴿"O Musa, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: The tree was a green acacia that was delicate. Qatadah said: a thorn bush. Wahb said: a bramble (ʿulayq).

﴿And throw down your staff.﴾ ﴿Then when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾, which is a small snake, because of the quickness of its movement, ﴿he turned and fled in retreat, and did not look back.﴾ Then it was said, "O Musa, come forward and do not fear. Indeed, you are among the secure. ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without harm.﴾" So it came out like a lamp. ﴿And draw your arm close to you from fear.﴾ Hafs read "al-rahb" with a fatha on the ra' and a jazm on the ha'. The people of Kufa and Syria read it with a damma on the ra' and a jazm on the ha'; others read it with a fatha on both the ra' and the ha'. Their evidence is the saying of Allah, glory be to Him: ﴿They called upon Us with hope and fear﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya: 60.]]. All of these readings have the same meaning: fear and dread.

The meaning of the verse: if the matter of your hand alarms you and you see its brightness, insert it into your pocket, and it will return to its former state. Some of them said: Allah commanded him to press his hand to his chest so that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, might remove what he had suffered of fear upon seeing the snake. It was also said: its meaning is to calm your fright and steady your heart, for it is the nature of one who is afraid that his heart is agitated and his body trembles. "Drawing in the wing" means calm. Qatadah said: a thorn bush. Wahb said: a bramble (ʿulayq).

﴿And throw down your staff.﴾ ﴿Then when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾, which is a small snake, because of the quickness of its movement, ﴿he turned and fled in retreat, and did not look back.﴾ Then it was said, "O Musa, come forward and do not fear. Indeed, you are among the secure. ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without harm.﴾" So it came out like a lamp. ﴿And draw your arm close to you from fear.﴾ Hafs read "al-rahb" with a fatha on the ra' and a jazm on the ha'. The people of Kufa and Syria read it with a damma on the ra' and a jazm on the ha'; others read it with a fatha on both the ra' and the ha'. Their evidence is the saying of Allah, glory be to Him: ﴿They called upon Us with hope and fear﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya: 60.]]. All of these readings have the same meaning: fear and dread.

The meaning of the verse: if the matter of your hand alarms you and you see its brightness, insert it into your pocket, and it will return to its former state. Some of them said: Allah commanded him to press his hand to his chest so that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, might remove what he had suffered of fear upon seeing the snake. It was also said: its meaning is to calm your fright and steady your heart, for it is the nature of one who is afraid that his heart is agitated and his body trembles. "Drawing in the wing" means calm. Similar is the saying of Allah, glory be to Him: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ [[Surah al-Isra: 24.]], meaning gentleness; and His saying: ﴿And lower your wing to those who follow you among the believers﴾ [[Surah al-Shu'ara: 215.]], i.e., be gentle with them and soften your side toward them. Al-Farra' said: by "wing" he meant his staff.

Some scholars of meanings said: "al-Rahb" means "the sleeve," in the dialect of Himyar and Banu Hanifah. It is related from al-Asma'i that he heard some Bedouins say to another: "Give me what is in your rahb." He said: I asked him about rahb, and he said: the sleeve. Its meaning according to this interpretation: draw your hand to you and take it out of the sleeve, because he had grasped the staff while his hand was in his sleeve.

﴿So these are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chieftains; indeed, they are a people who are defiant.﴾ "Fadhanika" is the reading of the common readers with a light nun. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a doubled nun, which is the dialect of Quraysh. There are four opinions on its form: it is said that the nun was doubled as a substitute for the dropped alif, and the meeting of two sukuns was not regarded, since the original form is "fadhanika," and the first alif was deleted because of the meeting of two sukuns. It is also said that the doubling is for emphasis, as they added the lam to that. It is also said that it was doubled to distinguish it from the form that drops in the idafah, since "dhan" is not used in idafah. It is also said that it distinguishes the dual of a declinable noun from it. Abu 'Ubayd said: Abu 'Amr used to restrict this letter to doubling, unlike any other dual in the Qur'an, and I think he did so because of the small number of letters in the word, so he read it with emphasis.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿fadhanika﴾ refers to the staff and the white hand, ﴿two proofs from your Lord﴾.

﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I killed a person among them, so I fear that they will kill me. And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent than me in speech and clearer in explanation, so send him with me as a helper to confirm me. Indeed, I fear that they will deny me."﴾ He said that because of the knot that was in his tongue. Isa ibn 'Umar and the people of Madinah dropped the hamza of "ridan" seeking lightness. ﴿"He will confirm me"﴾: the common readers read it with a jazm, while 'Asim and Hamzah read it with a raf', which is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. Whoever reads it with a jazm does so as a response to the request; whoever reads it with a raf' does so as a circumstantial clause, meaning a helper confirming, whose condition is confirmation, like the saying of Allah, glory be to Him: ﴿Our Lord, send down upon us a table from heaven, which will be a festival﴾, i.e., existing, a state directed toward the future.

﴿"Indeed I fear that they will deny me."﴾ He said: ﴿"We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will give you both authority, so they shall not reach you. By Our signs, you and those who follow you will be the victors."﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 28, verses 36–43:

﴿Then, when Musa came to them with Our clear signs, they said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we never heard of this among our forefathers, the earliest ones."﴾ And Musa said, ﴿"My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him, and whose will be the good outcome of the abode."﴾ The common reading is with the waw (wa-qala Musa). The people of Makkah read it without the waw, and it is so in their codices: "Rabbi a'lamu" (Rabbi a'lamu). In the manuscript it reads "al-batil" (falsehood) in place of "al-mahiq" (truth) versus "al-mubtil" (the one who spreads falsehood). The reading of "wa-man takunu lahu" [qara'a] with the ya' is by the people of Kufa, and the rest read it with the ta'. ﴿The good outcome of the abode﴾ means the praiseworthy final end in the Hereafter. ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ means the disbelievers will not prosper.

﴿Pharaoh said, "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself. So kindle for me, O Haman, over the clay, and make for me a tower, that I may look at the god of Musa, though I think he is among the liars."﴾ That is, bake for me the kiln-bricks. It is also said that he was the first to make kiln-fired bricks and to build with them.

The people of tafsir (ahl al-tafsir) [in the Isfahan copy: al-sir] said: When Pharaoh commanded his minister Haman to build the tower (sarh), Haman gathered the workers and craftsmen until fifty thousand builders assembled, apart from the followers, the hired hands, those who fired the bricks and plaster, those who carpentered the wood and doors, and those who hammered the nails. They raised it and built it up until it reached a height no building of any created being had reached since God created the heavens and the earth. God, may He be exalted, willed to test them with it. When they finished it, Pharaoh climbed up to it and commanded arrows to be shot toward the sky, and they returned to him stained with blood.

He said, "I have killed the god of Musa." They said, "If Pharaoh ascends it on mules..." Then God, may He be exalted, sent Jibril (peace be upon him) at sunset, and he struck it with his wing and cut it into three pieces. One piece fell on Pharaoh's army and killed a thousand men from them, one piece fell into the sea, and one piece fell in the west. No one who had worked on it survived without perishing. This is God's saying, ﴿"So kindle for me, O Haman, over the clay, and make for me a tower, that I may look at the god of Musa."﴾ That is, a palace, so that I may look at him and learn his condition.

﴿He thought him among the liars﴾ meaning Musa, in his claim that there is a god other than me and that he is His messenger. ﴿He and his soldiers were arrogant in the land without right, and they thought that to Us they would not be returned.﴾ ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers, and We cast them into the sea.﴾ That is, the yamm, meaning the sea. Qatadah said: it is a sea beyond Egypt called Asaf; God drowned them in it. ﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse,﴾ meaning sorrow and punishment, ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the ones disfigured (al-maqbuhin),﴾ meaning the detested. Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Kaysan said: the destroyed. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning those whose appearance is disfigured by blackness of face and blueness of eyes. The people of [lexicography] say: "qabbahahu Allah" and "qabbahahu" mean that He made him ugly. ﴿And We gave Musa the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations, as insights for the people, and guidance and mercy, that they might remember.﴾

We were informed by Shu'ayb ibn Muhammad, who said: We were informed by Makki ibn 'Abdan, who said: Ahmad ibn al-Azhar narrated to us, saying:

Rawh ibn 'Ubadah narrated to us, from 'Awf, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not destroy any people, generation, nation, or town with a punishment from the sky since He sent down the Torah upon the earth, except the town whose people were transformed into apes. Have you not seen that Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We gave Musa the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ to the end of the verse." [130] [Kanz al-Ummal: 2/33, no. 3020.]
